notes.h: Factors that determine what people need to wear
notes.b: Clothing requirements are the needs an outfit must meet, and they vary between people and situations. Working out which needs matter most is the first step in choosing what to buy.
points: Function: clothing must protect the body from weather, provide the movement an activity needs and be safe for the wearer's work or play. For example, a waterproof jacket needs a close-weave, water-repellent fabric so rain cannot soak through.

Climate and season decide the weight of fabric, the amount of covering and the need for waterproof or insulating layers, because the clothing has to keep the body comfortable in the weather it will meet.

Cost versus money available: a buyer weighs the price of a garment against their budget, and the purchase cost is balanced against durability and the number of times it will be worn, which is why a dearer, hardwearing garment can be better value.
Availability: clothing can only be bought if it is stocked in the shops or online in the right size, colour and style, so what a person wears is limited by what they can actually find.
Personal taste and body shape guide the choice of style, colour and fit, because people want clothes that suit them and feel comfortable.
Occasion and activity define the level of formality, such as a school uniform, work wear, sportswear or a wedding outfit.
notes.tip: Keep function (what the garment must do) separate from how it looks. If asked to describe how function influences choice, give protection, comfort or movement and one example, such as a waterproof jacket with a water-repellent close-woven fabric and covered fastenings.

notes.b: People do not choose clothes in isolation. The culture, beliefs and groups around them shape what feels right to wear.
points: Culture shapes modesty and dress codes, and it inspires designs, because each culture has its own standards of what is suitable to wear. Traditional dress such as the sari and pashmina shawl, and traditional embroidery motifs, are examples.
Religious and national traditions influence the clothing worn for ceremonies, festivals and rites of passage (the key events in life, such as a wedding or graduation).
Peer groups influence teenagers, who often adopt the styles and brands their friends wear to gain acceptance.
Status: clothing signals a person's rank, wealth or profession, so what someone wears tells others about their position.
Identification: uniforms show that a person belongs to a group or holds a role, such as the uniform of a nurse. The principle is that a uniform signals role.
notes.tip: Examiners ask how factors such as available money, climate and cultural influences affect clothing choice, so link each factor to its effect on what is chosen. Give the general rule that culture sets modesty and dress codes, with an example, rather than naming one example alone.

notes.h: Influences of the media, trendsetters and fashion
notes.b: Most people see what is fashionable long before they see it in a shop. The media, admired public figures and designers decide which styles spread.
points: Magazines, newspapers, television, film and advertising popularise fashion by showing what is worn, so people see new styles and want them.
Young people copy the clothes worn by actors, presenters, musicians and sports stars they admire.

Trendsetters are individuals or groups whose choices are copied by others, and they set the direction for the mass market. Examples are James Dean (jeans, white T-shirt, black leather jacket), Jackie Kennedy (A-line suit and pillbox hat) and Princess Diana.
Fashion houses and designers launch collections at seasonal shows, which are then copied by high street retailers.
Fashion is the currently accepted style, and it changes over time, so clothing that was fashionable in one decade can look dated in the next.
Trendsetters are people, fashion is the accepted style and a trend is a short-lived direction, so keep the three terms apart.
notes.tip: If asked to define trendsetters, say they are people whose clothes are copied and give a named example with what they wore. For how the media influences teenagers, name the media and say that teenagers copy the stars they admire.

notes.h: Social influences on design and construction (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Social conditions change what people want to wear, so designers and makers change the garments they produce.
points: Social conformity, the wish to fit in with a group, drives demand for common styles, because people buy what others around them are wearing.
Changes in women's status and in male roles have altered the silhouettes and tailoring that designers offer, so garments such as women's trouser suits became common.
notes.tip: Pair each influence with its effect on the garment (design, fabric, price or construction) rather than only naming it. Expect to give two or three developed points when asked how social influences affect clothing design.

notes.h: Economic influences on design and construction (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Money decides both what consumers can spend and what it costs to make a garment, so the economy shapes design and construction.
points: Prosperity encourages consumers to spend on fashion, including power dressing and luxury items, because they have more money to spare.
In a downturn, consumers buy simpler, more sombre and lower-cost clothing, and manufacturers use cheaper materials to keep prices down.
Production costs, including raw materials and labour, set the price a garment must be sold at.
notes.tip: For how the economy affects design and fashion, say that reduced spending leads to simpler, sombre styles and low-cost materials, and that investment supports CAD, new fibres and new designers. Give the effect on the garment each time.

notes.h: Industrial influences on design and construction (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Technology changes how garments are designed and made, and how quickly new styles reach buyers.
points: Computer-aided design (CAD) allows designers to develop patterns and styles on screen before production, so ideas can be tested without making a sample.
Advanced sewing machines, computerised cutting and mass production make garments faster and cheaper to make.
New and high-tech fibres and blends, such as stretch fibres and microfibres, create fabrics with new properties.
Media and communication allow new styles to reach markets around the world very quickly, for example through fashion shows and images shared by phone.
notes.tip: For technological influences, name CAD, new fabrics and finishes, and international fashion shows with images sent quickly to magazines, and say what each does to the garment or its price.

keyTerms.definition: A need that an outfit must meet, such as protection, comfort, occasion or budget.
A person or group whose clothing choices are copied by others and help set the direction of fashion.
The style accepted by a group of people at a particular time, which changes over time.
The use of computer software to design and develop garments and patterns on screen before production.
The tendency to adopt the clothing and behaviour of a group in order to fit in.
Formal, tailored clothing worn to project authority and status, typically in a business setting.
A very fine synthetic fibre that gives fabric a soft feel and can be used to make lightweight, durable garments.
A long piece of fabric wrapped around the body, traditional dress for many women in India.

factCards.definition: Function, cost versus money available, and availability of suitable clothing.

CAD, advanced sewing and cutting machinery, and new high-tech fibres.

factCards.term: Two ways the media influences clothing
factCards.definition: Magazines, television and film popularise styles, and young people copy the clothes worn by celebrities.
It determines modesty and traditional dress, and it inspires designs such as Russian fur trims and Indian saris.

factCards.definition: Trendsetters' choices are copied by others, and high street retailers then copy the styles that designers show at seasonal collections.

questions.prompt: Name three factors that influence what a person needs to wear, and give one example of each.
questions.model: Function: a waterproof jacket for a hiking trip protects against rain and wind. Cost versus money available: a student may buy a cheaper jumper that will be worn for one season, because their budget is limited. Availability: a person in a rural area may only find clothes in local shops, which limits their choice of size and style.

questions.prompt: Discuss how social, economic and industrial influences have shaped the design and construction of clothing.
questions.model: Social influences: conformity leads consumers to buy common styles that suit their peer group, and changes in the status of women and the role of men have altered the tailoring and silhouettes designers offer. Economic influences: when prosperity grows, consumers spend more on fashion, including power dressing and luxury items; in a recession, consumers buy simpler, more sombre clothing and manufacturers use cheaper materials, and production costs for raw materials and labour set the selling price. Industrial influences: CAD allows designers to develop styles and patterns on screen before production, advanced sewing machines and computerised cutting speed up construction, and new high-tech and microfibre materials create fabrics with new properties. Media and fast transport spread new styles quickly, so manufacturers can respond to demand rapidly.
